old_text: For block-programmed control of MuJoCo mechanics, I integrated the SNS blocks with the MathWorks MuJoCo--Simulink bridge. Actuator commands enter the mechanical simulation, and joint and actuator measurements return through its sensor interface. Local compatibility and initialization fixes establish the appropriate model state before signal exchange. The bridge retains the selected mechanical timestep and supports different controller and mechanical update rates. Neural and mechanical updates in the reported Gait2392 controller experiments use a \qty{2}{\milli\second} interval; bridge verification also tests a different stated rate combination. Each test retains its actual integration settings.

old_text: Mechanical inspection exposed faults that would otherwise have been attributed to controller behavior. Repairs addressed selected joint-action signs, active force scales, coupled path-point limits, and intended ground contacts. At matched poses and OpenSim static-optimization activations, eight of twelve sampled muscles had force-prediction $R^2$ between 0.87 and 0.98 and mean forces within \qty{10}{\percent} of the reference (Figure~\ref{fig:force-compare}; Table~\ref{tab:force-r2}). Rectus femoris and biceps femoris short head had negative $R^2$. Thus, the comparison identified useful agreement and important remaining muscle-specific differences. It assigned pose and activation frame by frame, without reproducing trajectory velocities or tendon dynamics, and consequently did not establish dynamic equivalence of the muscle formulations.

old_text: Bridge tests established that a block-programmed controller could deliver muscle commands and receive the corresponding measurements. Single-muscle activation, different control rates, and sensor readback were compared with Python MuJoCo integration. The five tested sensor signals were bit-exact over the scored 80-step window. A separate exported network drove all 92 actuator channels during a \qty{5}{\second} run, and a closed-loop reflex experiment exercised both command and sensory return. These results verify the interface operations under their stated conditions.
new_text: Bridge tests established that a block-programmed controller could deliver muscle commands and receive the corresponding measurements. Single-muscle activation, different control rates, and sensor readback were compared with Python MuJoCo integration. The five tested sensor arrays were bit-exact over 80 steps from \qty{0.005}{\second} to \qty{0.400}{\second}, excluding the initial sample. A separate exported network drove all 92 actuator channels during a \qty{5}{\second} run, and a closed-loop reflex experiment exercised both command and sensory return. These results verify the interface operations under their stated conditions.

old_text: For the contact-driven W2L rhythm core, identical neuron definitions, synapses, parameters, drive, and contact inputs were supplied to NumPy and Simulink implementations. Burst periods matched at \qty{1.000}{\second}, all ten expected bursts were reproduced, and voltage correlation was at least 0.99996 (Figure~\ref{fig:w2l_crossengine}). Removing the phasic heel input caused both realizations to latch. This verifies the tested circuit calculation and its dependence on the specified inputs, before introducing a different mechanical feedback history.

\begingroup\widowpenalty=10000\clubpenalty=10000
The contact-driven W2L comparison tested a representative 26-neuron Simulink rhythm core against the corresponding signals of the 95-neuron NumPy network. The core used corresponding neuron parameters and shared pathways under identical drive and prescribed heel inputs. Over the post-startup \qtyrange{2}{12}{\second} window, burst periods matched at \qty{1.000}{\second} and all ten expected bursts were reproduced. Best-lag correlation of the four shared RG voltage traces was at least 0.99996, allowing a \qty{2}{\milli\second} relative alignment lag (Figure~\ref{fig:w2l_crossengine}). Removing the phasic heel input caused both realizations to latch. This verifies the tested shared rhythm core and input dependence, rather than complete-network or unshifted sample agreement.\par

A \qty{2}{\nano\ampere}, \qty{100}{\milli\second} PF pulse during a silent phase changed its voltage without crossing the transmission threshold and produced essentially no MN response. During an active phase, the pulse changed PF voltage by up to \qty{1.14}{\milli\volt} and iliacus MN voltage by \qty{0.16}{\milli\volt}. old_text: A bounded syn6 gain-only repair improved its fitting loss but still passed none of the twelve channel checks. It was not accepted, and further downstream fitting was held pending a declared and verified PF design. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_pf_timing} retains the timing overlay and failed attempt. This finding is useful evidence for the workflow: an output fit can conceal an upstream design error, whereas inspecting the transmitted activity can identify it before further mechanical optimization.
new_text: A bounded syn6 gain-only repair improved its fitting loss but still passed none of the twelve channel checks. Subsequent RG-triggered relays and native SNS timing circuits addressed the failed function directly. The native circuit passed all 48 channel-cycle checks at the nominal cadence, and adaptive clocks extended that result to six controlled replay cadences. Those later checks evaluated individual cycles under additional onset and offset requirements; their denominator differs from the original twelve channel-mean checks. The improvement did not transfer directly to the live mechanical loop: coupled trials either reached the predictive knee guard or completed without satisfying the retained rhythm and PF-timing requirements. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_pf_timing} distinguishes the original failure, offline timing success, transmitted live behavior, and unsuccessful physical acceptance. Together these results show why an output fit and a favorable neural replay require separate checks before promotion to a coupled experiment.

old_text: The evidence is cumulative. Matched circuit calculations test implementation, the reduced reflex models test closed-loop transmission, and the air and ground demonstrations test selected coupled configurations. The PF timing failure further shows that the workflow can identify an unsuccessful design even when a downstream output fit appears acceptable. new_text: The evidence is cumulative. Matched circuit calculations test implementation, the reduced reflex models test closed-loop transmission, and the air and ground demonstrations test selected coupled configurations. The original PF timing failure shows that the workflow can identify an unsuccessful design even when a downstream output fit appears acceptable. Later timing repairs also show that an accepted intermediate computation can lose its intended behavior when live sensory return replaces prescribed replay inputs. This supports the dissertation objective of developing research tools rather than treating one visually favorable movement as the sole outcome.

old_text: Support conditions are equally important to interpretation. Air motion tests coordination without foot loading; supported ground tests introduce contact while retaining specified assistance. The current BiW2Lvar+ air stages, historical W2L feedback comparison, newer W2L108 ground result, and CAD hybrid-control result therefore demonstrate complementary capabilities without forming one continuous curriculum completed by a single controller.

The retained adapter defines stage 1 with sensory return disabled and sustained normalized flexor and extensor commands set to zero. It defines stage 2 with live sensory return enabled and each command set to 0.15 on both sides, consistent with the fitted command manifest. That adapter also defines the same initialization seed for both stages, an added 0.4 on the right extensor and left flexor command channels for the first 50 neural calls (\qty{100}{\milli\second}); this seed does not impose a continuing stride clock. It clamps the postural, balance, and functional-command channels off, sets direct tonic RG current to zero, and disables the legacy shared-drive input. The original launch adapter and complete consumed-command traces were not recovered; these are declared adapter settings rather than independently verified input samples from that launch. Thus these air stages cannot be treated as a matched feedback-only comparison. The retained shared descending drive in the separate historical weaning study below belongs to a different configuration.

new_text:
A bounded gain-only repair improved the mirrored-target objective and reproduced it in a new process, but still passed zero of twelve channels. It was not accepted or installed in the body adapter. Subsequent experiments changed the timing design rather than treating this failed repair as sufficient. RG-event-triggered relays first reproduced the intended windows in offline replay. A native SNS implementation then used onset, shutoff, quieting, follower, and ramp cells; an adaptive version adjusted its clock rates from recurrence of bilateral RG events. The adaptive implementation therefore combines graded neural computation with an explicit timing scheduler.

The later timing gate scores each of the last four complete ipsilateral RG-E intervals separately, at 200 phase samples per interval. Six channels on two sides give 48 channel-cycle checks. RG-E intervals begin at a \qty{3.5}{\milli\volt} crossing after arming below \qty{1.5}{\milli\volt}. In addition to the original lag, duty, burst-count, and excursion requirements, each onset and offset must lie within 0.05 cycles of its target. This differs from the original twelve checks on cycle-averaged channels. Table~\ref{tab:app_pf_progression} separates the resulting levels of verification. Cadence stress tests scale the legacy-cell integration and RG inactivation constants with the afferent replay cadence, while retaining native relay settings and MN synapses; they do not demonstrate spontaneous cadence adaptation by a freely moving model.
